To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

late career faculty are an important and growing population in academic medicine, and that the majority of faculty affairs and faculty development offices do not prioritize retirement planning and support for their late career faculty.

the majority of faculty affairs/faculty de-velopment offices do not have a formal retirement plan, and the most commonly reported resources for faculty retirement are emeritus status or honorific appointments.
the academic medicine community knows very little about the policies and programs for faculty in pre- and postretirement stages.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) identifying and describing the range of institutional policies, programs, resources, and services for late career faculty and retirement planning in medical schools; (2) understanding the perceived impact of institutional policies and programs on late career faculty and their decisions to retire; (3) identifying the perceived barriers to retirement planning and support; and (4), exploring the perceived impact of faculty affairs offices on the late career faculty and retirements.
the development of a model for the management of late-career faculty in the medical school setting.

the following questions: 1. What is known about late career faculty? 2. What are the current policies and practices regarding late career faculty in U.S. medical school? 3. How can faculty affairs and faculty development offices better serve late career faculty?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have provided a comprehensive and detailed survey of the current state of affairs regarding late career faculty in medical school.

the data from this survey highlight an important gap between the needs and priorities of late career faculty members and their institutions, and faculty affairs/faculty de-velopment offices must meet these needs and priorities.
late career and retirement planning and support is an important issue in medical schools, but it is a relatively low priority in the faculty affairs/faculty de velopment offices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of medical schools have no retirement policy and no formalized retirement planning.
the needs of the aging faculty population are not being addressed in a comprehensive way by the institutions.
we need to better understand and support faculty in all stages of their careers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the academic medicine community must develop a more comprehensive understanding of the needs of late career faculty, the policies and practices of their institutions, and the resources available to support them in their retirement planning and transition.
there is an urgent need for more data on the retirement patterns of late career faculty.
faculty affairs/faculty de velopment offices should be the hub for faculty support in pre and post-retirement.
